key_terms.meaning: A fluid is treated as continuous when the smallest length of interest is much larger than molecular spacing.
A hypothetical fluid with zero viscosity and no surface tension; it cannot support shear.
A fluid with viscosity and often surface tension; it resists shear and dissipates energy.
ρ = m/V, mass per unit volume, in kg/m³.
γ = ρg, weight per unit volume, in N/m³.
SG = ρ/ρ_water, ratio of density to that of water at 4 °C.
K = −Δp/(ΔV/V), resistance to volume change, in Pa.
β = 1/K = −(1/V)(ΔV/Δp), fractional volume change per unit pressure, in Pa⁻¹.
μ = τ/(du/dy), shear stress per unit velocity gradient, in Pa·s.
ν = μ/ρ, dynamic viscosity divided by density, in m²/s.
τ = μ du/dy for a Newtonian fluid; shear stress is proportional to velocity gradient.
A fluid whose viscosity μ is constant at a given temperature and pressure.
A fluid whose shear stress is not a straight-line function of shear rate through the origin.
σ = force/length along a liquid surface, in N/m; it makes the surface behave like a stretched membrane.
Rise or fall of liquid in a narrow tube due to surface tension and adhesion; h = 2σ cosθ/(ρgr).
p_abs = p_gauge + p_atm, pressure measured from absolute zero.
p_gauge = p_abs − p_atm, pressure measured above atmospheric pressure.
A U-tube or inclined tube device that measures pressure by balancing it against a liquid column; Δp = ρgΔh.
The point on a submerged surface where the resultant hydrostatic force acts.
GM = BM − BG, the distance between metacentre and centre of gravity; positive GM means stable floating equilibrium.

takeaways: A fluid can be modelled as a continuum when the flow scale is far larger than the molecular spacing, so density and velocity can be assigned to a point.
Density, specific weight and specific gravity are simple ratios of mass, weight and water density; bulk modulus and compressibility describe volume change under pressure.
Viscosity converts velocity differences between layers into shear stress; Newton's law of viscosity is τ = μ du/dy.
Newtonian fluids have constant viscosity, while non-Newtonian fluids change apparent viscosity with shear rate.
Surface tension causes a pressure jump across a curved interface and produces capillary rise or fall in narrow tubes.
In a static fluid, pressure increases linearly with depth, and gauge pressure is absolute pressure minus atmospheric pressure.
A manometer uses the same-fluid-same-level rule: equal levels in the same continuous fluid have equal pressure.
The resultant force on a plane submerged surface is pressure at the centroid times area, and it acts at the centre of pressure.
Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid; a floating body is stable when its metacentric height is positive.
For a curved submerged surface, horizontal and vertical force components can be found separately; the vertical component equals the weight of the displaced liquid column.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask you to define the property, draw the pressure diagram and then compute force, centre of pressure or stability, so show the formula, substitution and units.

bank.q: Define a fluid as a continuum. Distinguish between ideal and real fluids. State one practical situation where the continuum assumption is not valid and explain why.
outline: Definition of continuum: length scale of interest much larger than molecular spacing
Ideal fluid: inviscid and incompressible; real fluid: has viscosity
Example where continuum fails: very small channel or low-pressure gas
Reason: molecular spacing becomes comparable to the flow dimension

bank.q: Define density, specific weight and specific gravity. Write the relation for bulk modulus and compressibility, and explain what a large bulk modulus means for a liquid.
outline: ρ = m/V; γ = ρg; SG = ρ/ρ_water
K = −Δp/(ΔV/V); β = 1/K
Large K means small volume change for a given pressure change
Units: kg/m³, N/m³, Pa, Pa⁻¹

bank.q: State Newton's law of viscosity. Draw and explain rheograms for Newtonian, shear-thinning and shear-thickening fluids.
outline: τ = μ du/dy and meaning of μ and du/dy
Newtonian: straight line through origin
Shear-thinning: apparent viscosity falls as shear rate rises
Shear-thickening: apparent viscosity rises as shear rate rises

bank.q: Explain surface tension and capillarity. Derive the capillary rise h in a tube of radius r and state the meaning of each symbol.
outline: Surface tension as force per length at the liquid surface
Pressure jump across a curved meniscus
Force balance: 2πrσ cosθ = ρgπr²h
h = 2σ cosθ/(ρgr); define σ, θ, ρ, g and r

bank.q: A pipe carries water. A U-tube manometer with mercury is connected to it. Given the levels and fluid densities, calculate the gauge pressure in the pipe.
outline: Start from the pipe pressure and move down and up the manometer
Use p = p₀ + ρgh for each fluid column
Apply same-fluid-same-level rule at the mercury interface
Substitute densities, g and level differences; report gauge pressure in Pa or kPa

bank.q: A vertical rectangular gate of width b and height h holds water on one side. Find the total hydrostatic force and the depth of the centre of pressure.
outline: F = ρg h_c A, where h_c is depth to centroid
Area A = b h and h_c = h/2 for the gate top at the free surface
Centre of pressure depth h_p = h_c + I_c/(A h_c)
I_c = b h³/12; compute h_p below the free surface

bank.q: An inclined circular gate of diameter d is submerged in water at angle θ. Find the resultant force and its location along the plane.
outline: F = ρg h_c A with h_c measured vertically to the centroid
A = πd²/4; find vertical depth of centroid from geometry
Use y_p = y_c + I_c/(A y_c) along the plane
I_c = πd⁴/64; convert y_p to vertical depth if needed

bank.q: A wooden block floats in water. Given its volume and mass, find the volume displaced and the specific gravity of the wood.
outline: Buoyant force equals weight of block
ρ_water g V_displaced = m g
V_displaced = m/ρ_water
SG_wood = ρ_wood/ρ_water = m/(ρ_water V_block)

bank.q: A cylindrical buoy of diameter D and height H floats in seawater. Find its metacentric height and state whether it is stable.
outline: Find submerged depth from weight balance
BM = I/V, with I = πD⁴/64 and V displaced
Locate centre of buoyancy B and centre of gravity G
GM = BM − BG; positive GM means stable

bank.q: A capillary tube of small radius is dipped in a liquid. Calculate the capillary rise for given surface tension, contact angle and density, and find the tube diameter for a specified rise.
outline: Use h = 2σ cosθ/(ρgr)
Substitute σ, θ, ρ, g and r
For a specified h, rearrange to r = 2σ cosθ/(ρgh)
Diameter = 2r; check units

bank.q: Compare piezometer, U-tube manometer, inverted U-tube manometer and inclined manometer. For a low gas pressure and for a small liquid pressure difference, choose a suitable instrument and justify.
outline: Piezometer: simple, only for liquids, limited range
U-tube: wide range, suitable for gases and liquids
Inverted U-tube: useful for small pressure differences with light fluid
Inclined manometer: magnifies small differences and increases sensitivity
Choice depends on fluid, range, sensitivity and whether gas or liquid

bank.q: A curved gate holds water. Determine the horizontal and vertical components of the hydrostatic force and their lines of action. Discuss how the result changes if the water level rises.
outline: Horizontal component equals force on vertical projection
Vertical component equals weight of fluid above or below the curved surface
Locate each component through centre of pressure or centroid of displaced volume
Resultant from vector addition; line of action through intersection
Rising water level increases both components and may change direction of vertical force

bank.q: Derive the condition GM = BM − BG for a floating body. A barge has its centre of gravity raised; evaluate how this affects stability.
outline: Define metacentre M and centre of buoyancy B
For small tilt, BM = I/V
GM = BM − BG
Positive GM: stable; zero: neutral; negative: unstable
Raising G reduces GM and can make the barge unstable

bank.q: A tank contains two immiscible liquids. A manometer is connected at the side and a vertical gate is fitted at the bottom. Find the pressure at the gate top, the force on the gate, and the manometer reading. State assumptions.
outline: Pressure at depth: p = p_atm + Σρg h for each layer
Force on gate: F = p_c A with p_c at gate centroid
Centre of pressure from I_c/(A y_c)
Manometer: balance pressure using same-fluid-same-level rule
Assume static fluid, sharp interface, known densities and atmospheric pressure on free surface

glossary.def: A model in which fluid properties are assumed to vary smoothly from point to point, ignoring individual molecules.
Mass per unit volume of a fluid, measured in kg/m³.
Weight per unit volume of a fluid, equal to ρg and measured in N/m³.
The ratio of a fluid's density to the density of water at 4 °C.
The pressure increase needed to produce a unit fractional decrease in volume.
The reciprocal of bulk modulus; fractional volume change per unit pressure change.
The fluid property that relates shear stress to velocity gradient, measured in Pa·s.
Dynamic viscosity divided by density, measured in m²/s.
Tangential force per unit area acting between fluid layers.
The rate at which velocity changes with distance perpendicular to the flow direction.
A fluid in which shear stress is directly proportional to shear rate at a given temperature.
A fluid in which the relation between shear stress and shear rate is not a straight line through the origin.
The force per unit length acting along a liquid surface, tending to reduce surface area.
The rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube caused by surface tension and contact angle.
The angle between the liquid surface and the solid wall at the contact line.
Pressure measured from absolute zero, equal to gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure.
Pressure measured relative to atmospheric pressure, equal to absolute pressure minus atmospheric pressure.
The amount by which pressure is below atmospheric pressure; it is a negative gauge pressure.
An instrument that measures pressure by balancing it against a column of liquid.
A simple vertical tube open to atmosphere, used to measure pressure in a liquid pipeline.
The point where the resultant hydrostatic force acts on a submerged surface.
The upward force exerted by a fluid on a body immersed in it, equal to the weight of displaced fluid.
The point where the vertical line through the new centre of buoyancy meets the original vertical centreline after a small tilt.
The distance between the metacentre and the centre of gravity of a floating body.
A floating body condition in which a small tilt produces a restoring moment; metacentric height is positive.
The force exerted by a static fluid on a submerged surface, equal to pressure at the centroid times area for a plane surface.
